Title: A Kubernetes CVE just dropped. Here’s how to find and fix what matters.

Full Text:
Critical Kubernetes CVEs arrive constantly. Some hit an operator or controller, some the Linux kernel underneath your nodes, others the container images your teams ship every day. Each one comes with a CVSS score and an urgent recommendation to patch.

What it doesn’t come with is context. A CVSS score tells you how bad a flaw could be in theory. It can’t tell you whether the vulnerable component runs in your clusters, whether anyone could actually exploit it, or what it can reach. Without those answers, teams either scramble to patch everything at once or let the CVE sit in a backlog until it’s forgotten.

Kubernetes makes this harder than most environments. Workloads are ephemeral, permissions are spread across roles, bindings and service accounts, and a single foothold can travel from a pod to a node, from a node to the cloud account, or through a privileged operator to everything it manages.

This post walks through a repeatable approach for triaging any Kubernetes CVE in Orca, then puts it to work on a real example: Copy Fail, a Linux kernel flaw affecting nodes across nearly every major cloud and operating system.

How to triage a Kubernetes CVE: Four questions to ask

Whatever the CVE, effective triage comes down to the same four questions. Orca answers each one from a single platform for cloud security, across every cluster and the cloud accounts they run in.

Where does it run?

Is it internet exposed?

Is it exploitable?

What can it reach?

Each answer narrows the list for the next, so a CVE that touches dozens of clusters ends with a short, ranked set of actions. Here’s how that looks on a real example.

The example: Copy Fail (CVE-2026-31431)

Copy Fail is a bug in the Linux kernel that lets an ordinary user quietly give themselves full admin (root) access. In Kubernetes, that means an attacker who gets into any container can take over the node it runs on, and from there, potentially everything that node can reach. Here’s how Orca takes you from the headline to a fix.

Step 1: Find which nodes and images are affected

Orca’s emerging threats feed, From the News, flags Copy Fail with a plain-language summary and recommended fix. From there, search CVE-2026-31431 in the Vulnerabilities view, part of Orca’s agentless vulnerability management, to see every affected node, node pool and image across clusters and clouds, with the fixed kernel version for each.

Prefer plain English? Ask Orca AI, an AI reasoning engine for security teams, “Which Kubernetes nodes are affected by CVE-2026-31431?” and get the same answer in seconds.

Step 2: Check whether affected nodes or pods are internet exposed

Copy Fail needs a foothold inside a pod first, so checking the node alone isn’t enough. A node can sit on a private network and still run a pod that’s reachable from the internet through a LoadBalancer or an Ingress. If that pod is compromised, the attacker lands on the node’s kernel just the same. Click into an affected node to see its asset details, including whether the node or any workload running on it is publicly accessible, and how many high-severity risks it carries. Nodes with any internet-facing path go to the top of the list. Nodes with no exposure still get patched, just on a normal cycle.

Step 3: Confirm whether the CVE is exploitable

Open the Copy Fail risk on that node to see the vulnerable kernel package it affects, along with Orca’s exploitability and risk scoring details. Copy Fail has public exploit code, so the answer is yes, and on a node with an internet-exposed workload, that moves it from “patch soon” to “patch now.”

Step 4: Map the attack path from node to cloud

A node escape is only as dangerous as what the node can access. Use attack path analysis to see how an attacker could move to the cloud roles, secrets or crown jewel data within reach, all in one ranked path. That’s the alert you patch first.

Go further with Orca: Remediate, prevent, and prove progress

That’s the triage done. But finding the risk is only part of the job, and Orca helps with the rest too.

Prove progress to leadership. When leadership asks where things stand, you shouldn’t need to scramble and pull a spreadsheet together to answer. The K8s & Container Security dashboard shows how many clusters and nodes are still affected, and that number drops as patches roll out, so one view shows both your current risk and your progress.

Patch without letting new risk in. Teams keep deploying while patches roll out, and every new pod is a possible foothold. Orca’s Admission Controller checks each workload before it’s admitted, stopping new privileged or host-namespace pods, which make it easier to take over a node from a compromised container, from landing in affected clusters. Policies can warn or block depending on what you need, and every decision is logged in Orca alongside the CVE you’re tracking.

Stay audit-ready. An unpatched critical vulnerability is an audit finding waiting to happen. Orca automatically maps it to the regulatory compliance frameworks you report on, such as PCI DSS 4.0 and SOC 2, so you know which controls are affected now and have the evidence ready once remediation is done, instead of scrambling for it later.

Cut the time to fix. Orca opens tickets in tools you already use with the affected nodes and fixed kernel version already filled in, so engineers start fixing instead of investigating, and you can track every ticket through to closure. Where patching has to wait, disabling the affected kernel module is a quick interim mitigation.

Catch an attack before the patch lands. Rolling new images across a fleet takes time, and that window is when attackers move. Orca’s cloud detection and response monitors affected workloads for suspicious activity, so if someone tries to use the foothold, you know right away and can respond.

Together, that’s the difference between knowing about a CVE and being done with it.

A repeatable workflow for the next Kubernetes CVE

Kubernetes CVEs aren’t slowing down, and patching everything the moment it’s disclosed isn’t realistic. The teams that stay ahead are the ones that know where those CVEs are throughout their environment, and which ones need to get remediated first.

Orca helps you do exactly that. From the first alert to the closed ticket, the Orca Cloud Security Platform shows you where a CVE runs, whether it’s exposed, whether it’s exploitable, what it can reach, and how it affects your compliance posture. Copy Fail is one example. The same workflow works for whatever CVE lands next.

Title: Who Holds the Keys to Your ChatGPT Workspace?
Context: Verizon’s 2026 DBIR found shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action, up 4x in a year, and a sanctioned tool is the best way to get people off personal...
Full Text:
Picture a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace a year after rollout. The IT lead who bought the licenses is still an Owner. So are the two admins she added during a busy week, and the director who asked for access “just to check something.” A contractor who left in the spring still has an account, because he was added by hand instead of through the identity provider. And a service account someone set up to run Codex jobs has a credential that never expires.

None of this is unusual. It’s what happens when a tool goes from pilot to every department in a few months, and nobody’s job is to keep an eye on the admin console.

Most of the security conversation around ChatGPT is about what people paste into it, and that’s fair. OpenAI’s Compliance Platform lets DLP and data security tools read conversations. But a more basic question usually goes unanswered: who actually holds the keys to the workspace?

Why nobody owns this

ChatGPT Enterprise falls between teams, so each one assumes someone else is watching it:

Identity teams own the identity provider, but SCIM provisioning to ChatGPT is optional. Anyone added directly in the admin console never shows up in their access reviews.

Cloud security teams own AWS, Azure, and GCP. A ChatGPT workspace isn’t a cloud account, so their CNAPP never sees it.

The workspace owner is usually whoever bought the licenses. Owner access gets handed out to get things done, and it rarely gets taken back.

Rolling out an enterprise AI platform is still the right call. Verizon’s 2026 DBIR found shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action, up 4x in a year, and a sanctioned tool is the best way to get people off personal accounts. But someone still has to check how that tool is set up.

What Orca checks in ChatGPT Enterprise

You connect ChatGPT Enterprise to Orca with one read-only Admin API key. There’s nothing to install and no change to how anyone uses ChatGPT. Orca pulls in every user, group, service account, and service-account credential in the workspace, and flags issues like these out of the box:

Orca detects

Why it matters

A user with the workspace Owner role

Owners control every setting, member and key in the workspace. Each one is a high-value account

A workspace with more than three owners

Owner access tends to spread and rarely gets revoked. The same rule applies to Azure subscriptions and Supabase

A service-account credential with no expiration date

A token that never expires stays valid long after the job or person that needed it is gone

A service-account credential not rotated in 90 days

OpenAI suggests token lifetimes of 7 to 90 days. Older tokens have had more time to leak

A user not provisioned through the identity provider

Users added by hand skip your joiner-mover-leaver process, so offboarding may never reach them

A group managed by hand instead of synced from the identity provider

Manual groups drift from the access you approved in the IdP

A group with no members

Empty groups are leftovers that can quietly grant access to the next person added

ChatGPT belongs next to the rest of your risk

An AI-built app has five parts: the model behind it, the agent or builder that made it, the platform it runs on, the database and login behind it, and the cloud account under it. Each comes from a different vendor and has a different owner. None of those owners is security.

Orca AI AppGen Security brings those parts into one platform. ChatGPT Enterprise sits next to Claude Enterprise at the model layer, alongside Vercel and your AWS, Azure, and GCP accounts.

A DLP tool reads chats, a secrets scanner finds OpenAI API keys in repos, and the CNAPP covers Azure OpenAI.

Each tool sees its own piece, so nobody can say how exposed the company is to OpenAI overall. In Orca, ChatGPT users, groups, and credentials sit in the same inventory as OpenAI API keys found in code and container images, workloads calling OpenAI models (seen by the Orca Sensor), and Azure OpenAI resources. They land in the same queue as your Claude Enterprise and Vercel findings, too.

Title: CVE-2026-101767: Critical Oracle EBS SQL Injection Actively Probed in the Wild
Context: CVE-2026-101767 disclosure and exploitation timeline The vulnerability was discovered by Horizon3
Full Text:
What is CVE-2026-101767?

A critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-101767, CVSS 9.8) was disclosed affecting Oracle E-Business Suite’s Application Object Library, allowing attackers to achieve full remote code execution and system takeover via an unauthenticated SQL injection in the Thin Client Framework servlet. Due to the potential for complete compromise of financial, payroll, and HR data managed by EBS, immediate patching is required.

How the Oracle EBS SQL injection leads to remote code execution

The issue originates from the Application Object Library’s TCF servlet at /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer, where missing authentication on a critical function combined with improper input sanitization leads to SQL injection as the privileged APPS database user. By sending specially crafted POST requests to the servlet instantiating oracle.apps.jtf.gantt.server.GanttDataServer, attackers can execute arbitrary SQL commands and chain to operating system command execution as the EBS application account, potentially achieving full takeover of the EBS instance and all data it manages. No authentication is required to exploit this issue.

CVE-2026-101767 disclosure and exploitation timeline

The vulnerability was discovered by Horizon3.ai and reported to Oracle on July 24, 2026. Oracle addressed it in the October 2026 Critical Patch Update, released October 20. Within a week of the patch release, threat intelligence firm Defused observed exploratory exploitation attempts hitting Oracle EBS honeypots on October 27. EBS has historically been a target for financially motivated threat actors, including the Cl0p group’s large-scale EBS campaign the previous year.

Which Oracle E-Business Suite versions are affected?

The following components are affected: Oracle E-Business Suite Application Object Library, versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15. Oracle notes that earlier unsupported versions are likely also affected. The vulnerable servlet passes through the default EBS URL firewall configuration, meaning any internet-facing EBS instance with default settings is exposed. Organizations running EBS for financial, payroll, HR, and procurement operations face elevated risk due to the sensitive data accessible through the APPS database user.

How to patch and mitigate CVE-2026-101767

Users should apply the October 2026 Critical Patch Update immediately (details in My Oracle Support Note KA923), and also patch the underlying EBS Database and Fusion Middleware components, which have separate CPU entries. As interim mitigations until patching is complete, administrators should remove /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer from the EBS URL firewall allowlist and restrict network access to the EBS web tier to trusted networks only.

Is CVE-2026-101767 being exploited in the wild?

At the time of writing, Horizon3.ai has published technical details of the attack chain, and active probing has been confirmed in the wild by Defused. The vulnerability is not yet listed on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Regardless, the severity and ease of exploitation make this vulnerability high risk, especially in internet-facing deployments.

What attackers can do with a compromised Oracle EBS instance

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to execute arbitrary SQL and OS commands as the APPS and EBS application accounts, exfiltrate or manipulate sensitive financial, payroll, and HR data, and potentially pivot to other systems within the network, leading to service disruption, data exposure, or full infrastructure compromise.

How Orca helps find and prioritize vulnerable Oracle EBS assets

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable versions of Oracle E-Business Suite, understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability, and asset criticality, and prioritize remediation based on real risk rather than CVSS alone. Orca’s platform highlights affected assets directly in the newItem view, helping security teams focus on the most critical remediation paths first

Title: Securing Vercel at Scale: From One Team to Every Team
Context: Researchers at Red Access found about 5,000 corporate apps among 380,000 public assets on AI app platforms, and about 40% of those exposed sensitive data (TechTarget)
Full Text:
On Thursday, a customer marketing manager vibe codes a community portal where customers can sign in, post questions, and search past answers. By Friday it’s live on Vercel, with a custom domain, an OPENAI_API_KEY for the AI search saved as a plain config variable, and a database full of customer names, emails, and support threads.

No ticket. No code review. No security sign-off. Nothing broke, so nobody looked.

Vercel has the settings to prevent every part of that. The harder question belongs to the security team: how do you know those settings are on, for every team, across the whole company?

The builder population just changed

Vercel used to be where front-end engineers shipped Next.js apps. Now it’s where AI ships apps for everyone else. Vercel’s v0 has crossed 4 million users (SaaStr), and CEO Guillermo Rauch says more than 60% of activity on Vercel is now driven by coding agents (The Stack).

Many of those apps belong to companies, not hobbyists. Researchers at Red Access found about 5,000 corporate apps among 380,000 public assets on AI app platforms, and about 40% of those exposed sensitive data (TechTarget).

Why your current tools only see part of it

Vercel isn’t a cloud account, a repo, or a typical SaaS app. It’s a control plane that sits between all three, so each tool you already own sees only part of it:

CNAPP sees the AWS, Azure, or GCP accounts DevOps provisioned. Vercel isn’t one of them.

AppSec scans the repos you point it at. An app built from a prompt may never pass through one.

SSPM checks SaaS sign-in and access settings, but rarely Vercel’s deployment and firewall settings.

Vercel’s own Security Dashboard, free on every plan since August 2026, is the best place to start. It scores a team on settings like MFA, owner count, token expiry, and secret storage (Vercel). But it covers one team at a time, a fixed list of checks, and only Vercel.

These settings are configured in Vercel, team by team, usually by whoever created the team: access tokens, environment variables, custom domains, deployment protection, SAML enforcement, firewall rules. That person usually isn’t on the security team.

Vercel’s dashboard tells one team how its settings look. Security teams need every team, more checks, and one place to work them next to the rest of their risk.

What Orca adds beyond Vercel’s dashboard

The integration supports Vercel Enterprise. You connect it with a Full Account access token created by a dedicated service user with the Enterprise Viewer and Security roles, so Orca’s access stays read-only. Set an expiration on the token and rotate it (Vercel access tokens). If your organization enforces SAML, connect each team with its own team token instead. There’s no agent to install, nothing to deploy in Vercel, and no change to how anyone builds.

Orca inventories every team the token can reach, including teams added later: projects, deployments, domains, members, access tokens, firewall settings, and environment-variable metadata, never the values. Each Vercel team shows up as an account in Orca, so you see every team in one place instead of one dashboard per team.

Orca runs a variety of detections out of the box. Some overlap with Vercel’s dashboard.

Four misconfigurations that AI-built apps make by default

These four issues come up most with AI-built apps. None is a mistake anyone makes on purpose. Each is a default, or a step builders skip because nothing breaks without it.

Production URLs with no login. Vercel’s Deployment Protection covers preview URLs by default. Production is a separate setting. Builders rarely change it, because the app works fine either way. The result is a public, indexable production URL with nothing in front of it. The fix is free: since September 2026, every plan can put Vercel Authentication in front of production and make it the team default (Vercel).

Secrets saved as readable Config variables. Since August 2026, Vercel stores each variable as Config (readable) or Secret (write-only) (Vercel). Values are encrypted at rest, but a STRIPE_SECRET_KEY saved as Config stays readable to anyone with project access. The name is the giveaway, and that’s what Orca flags.

SAML connected but not enforced. The identity team links the IdP to Vercel. Nobody turns on enforcement, so members can still reach the team without a SAML session (Vercel).

Long-lived and forgotten access tokens. A Full Account or Team token carries the role of the person who created it. Tokens set to never expire, or unused for 90 days, are standing credentials nobody is watching. Orca flags both. Project-scoped tokens limit any one token to a single project (Vercel).

One queue for every team

A dashboard per Vercel team works for the person who owns that team. It doesn’t work for a security team responsible for dozens of them.

In Orca, Vercel findings show up alongside your AWS, Azure, and GCP findings, in the same risk scoring, alert workflows, and ticketing integrations your team already uses. Each finding shows which Vercel team owns the project, so it reaches someone who can fix it. New teams are covered as soon as they’re created, without anyone registering them.

Vercel findings land prioritized in the same queue as your cloud findings in the Orca Platform

Vercel is one part of the AI-built app

An AI-built app has five parts: the model behind it, the agent or builder that made it, the platform it runs on, the database and login behind it, and the cloud account under it. Each comes from a different vendor and has a different owner. None of those owners is security.

Orca AI AppGen Security covers these parts in one platform instead of one tool per vendor. Today that means Vercel, where AI-built apps run, and Claude Enterprise, where many of them start, in the same inventory and the same queue. More platforms are coming.

The goal isn’t to slow builders down. They keep the tools they picked. Security gets enough visibility to say yes instead of no.

Title: PHP2Shell: From the attacker’s perspective
Context: How far AI got us We tried to build the attack ourselves, with AI, working only from the published repair and our own test servers
Full Text:
Executive Summary:

Two faults in PHP, the software behind roughly seven out of ten websites, let a stranger on the internet run commands on a web server. A repair was published on 21 October.

We downloaded an attack tool that a stranger had published on GitHub and ran it, unchanged, against our own test server running an ordinary, unrepaired installation of PHP and it successfully took control.

We then built our own exploit with AI, starting from the published fix. Within hours, it ran commands on a standard PHP server – and worked against an ordinary WordPress site too.

What are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619?

Why PHP vulnerabilities put most of the web at risk

When you open a web page, something has to build that page before it reaches you. For roughly seven out of ten websites, the software doing that job is PHP. It sits on the web server, assembles the page, and sends it to your browser. It is underneath WordPress, Drupal, Magento and a great many ordinary company websites.

What went wrong

CVE-2026-109618 leaves PHP’s internal state corrupted when its memory limit is reached, allowing attackers to hijack execution during cleanup. Its companion, CVE-2026-109619, causes a double free that exploit chains use to leak memory and defeat ASLR. Together, they can enable unauthenticated code execution and expose secrets; the fixes make allocation failures safe.

What we did

The question we wanted to answer was a practical one. How easy is it to create a working exploit with AI? And the answer is, it can get challenging. The guardrails of the modern models are strong and prevent the creation of a full-chain RCE exploit. But at the same time, they can always be bypassed. And none-the-less successful attack tools for this were still circulating within hours of the repair. The publishers are skilled hackers, and they were probably relying on local / non-guardrailed AI models.

How far AI got us

We tried to build the attack ourselves, with AI, working only from the published repair and our own test servers. AI found a way to make an ordinary web request use up all the memory PHP is allowed, on a server with entirely normal settings, before the website’s own code has even started. On the repaired version the same request is handled normally.

We then ran into tiring guardrails when attempting to ask for a full-chain RCE together with a memory leak primitive, and decided to switch to a different agent at this point. Once changed to another less restricted agent, it broke into a standard PHP server and ran commands in a matter of hours. Same attack then worked against an ordinary WordPress site.

successful exploit on 8.4.26

failed exploit on 8.4.27

Are AI-generated PHP exploits on GitHub a real threat?

The argument going round is that there are thousands of attack tools on GitHub, almost none of them work against a normal server, so the whole thing is overblown.

Most of those tools really are junk, written with AI by people with no way to tell whether they worked. Both things are true at once, though: the junk exists, and so do real attacks built with the same tools by people who check their results.

The speed is what to notice. When a similar flaw was found in another widely used program years ago, researchers were handed a full explanation of it and still took about three days to produce one working attack, against one specific version. Here nobody outside the disclosure knew what the flaw even was, and working attacks appeared within a day.

What made the difference was not a cleverer AI. It was the setup. That is the part to plan around. The flaw is still fiddly, and each version of PHP needs its own adjustments – but that is now a matter of leaving an AI to work through them, rather than a specialist’s week. The step from one broken server to several hundred has become a short one.

Why repairs help attackers too

A public fix also gives attackers a map of the flaw. PHP’s patch changed 300 files and included 127 regression tests designed to trigger the bugs – giving attackers expert-written examples to study. This is the same exact problem we’ve re-iterated with BGH. With vulnerable versions still available, anyone can compare behavior before and after the fix, just as we did. Publication starts the race: defenders must patch while attackers turn those clues into working exploits.

An unexpected finding

Working attacks existed before the flaw was public at all, with AI and nothing but the scraps already circulating. AI closed the gap between knowing a flaw exists and having a one-command tool, and that the internet then improved that tool for free. The window defenders assume they have, between a repair appearing and attacks following, can close before the repair is announced. This is a true game-changer in patch security.

How to protect PHP servers from CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

Update PHP wherever you run it. We verified that the repair stops this attack. Versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12 and later contain it.

Find out where you run it. The harder half of the problem for most organisations is not patching, it is knowing which servers to patch. Old marketing sites, acquired brands, forgotten test machines and suppliers’ systems are where this will land.

If a server cannot be updated, take it off the public internet. Older versions of PHP have no repair available at all. For those, removing public access is the only real answer.

Assume that anything exposed and unpatched may already have been reached, and check it rather than hoping. Attempts against this were seen before the repair existed.

Title: PHP2Shell: What This Week Tells Us About the Web We Built

Full Text:
The week the web’s plumbing failed

On Wednesday afternoon, most of the world’s websites became exploitable at the same moment. The reason was PHP, the thirty-year-old language that still serves roughly seven out of ten sites you visit, including nearly every WordPress, Drupal, Magento and Joomla deployment on earth.

Two bugs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, now known collectively as PHP2Shell, let an unauthenticated attacker run code on any server that handles PHP web requests. They are present in every PHP version back to 5.4, released in 2012. The coordinated disclosure broke down a day early, after leaks on 20 October. Exploit attempts hit honeypots before a patch existed. Government sites in Europe chose to go dark on patch day rather than stay online and exposed.

I have watched a great many “critical” bulletins come and go. Most of them deserve a calm Tuesday and a ticket in the queue. This one does not, and I want to explain why in business terms rather than technical ones. The technical story will be told well by the researchers who found it, and our own research team at Orca has published its analysis. The business story is the one your board, your CFO and your customers are going to ask you about.

What happened

The two flaws sit in the parts of PHP that every request touches: memory management and error handling. CVE-2026-109618 abuses how PHP bails out of an out-of-memory condition while request data is only half initialised. CVE-2026-109619 abuses global state that keeps pointing at request memory after that memory has been freed. Both are rated 9.2 on CVSS v4 and work without credentials, and both can also be used to read process memory, which is where your database passwords, API keys and session secrets happen to live.

What makes this different from the usual PHP advisory is the discovery story. The out-of-memory weakness was first noticed in 2020 and rediscovered during an audit in 2024. Nobody could prove it was exploitable, so it was never fixed. In August 2026, a small group of researchers, among them Calif and OpenAI, used frontier AI models to build the exploit chain that human researchers had judged impractical. The flaw did not change. The cost of proving it had.

Then the disclosure process came apart. A video with a working proof of concept was published by mistake. A container vendor shipped fixed images six hours before the coordinated release, giving anyone who cared to look a binary diff of the patch. The PHP Foundation pulled its release forward by a day. By the time the fixes landed, proof-of-concept exploits were already circulating and several vendors were watching attempts against their sensors.

The PHP team’s own position is blunt: there are no complete mitigations and updating is the only safe choice. Configuration tweaks can narrow specific attack paths. They do not close the hole.

Censys counts roughly 2.58 million internet-facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP. Every one of them that serves web requests, whether through PHP-FPM, mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP or LiteSpeed, is in scope.

Why this one hurts

The first thing to understand is that this is an engine bug, so every WordPress site, Drupal install and plugin inherits it. “Our application code is secure” is a true statement that does not matter. If your code runs on PHP, your code is the delivery vehicle for someone else’s payload.

The second thing is that almost nobody knows how much PHP they run. The flagship e-commerce platform, yes. The marketing microsite the agency built in 2019, the acquired brand’s storefront that was never migrated, the internal wiki, the staging box someone exposed to test a webhook, the customer portal your SaaS vendor runs on a hosting provider you have never heard of: these are the servers that will be compromised. Most of them are not in a CMDB. Many of them are not in anyone’s memory.

The third thing is what the attacker gets. The natural outcome of PHP2Shell is a web shell: a persistent backdoor living inside a legitimate, trusted, SSL-certified site that carries your brand. From there an attacker phishes your customers from your own domain, serves malware from a URL that every security product trusts, and reads credentials out of process memory to pivot into the cloud accounts behind the site. The breach does not look like a breach. It looks like your website.

The fourth thing is the patch itself. For PHP 8.2 and above there is a clean update. For 7.4 through 8.1 there are source backports, which means someone has to compile them. For anything older there is nothing at all. A great many enterprises are running end-of-life PHP underneath applications nobody wants to touch, because the last time someone touched them the site broke. Those organisations are now choosing between a planned outage and an unplanned compromise. That is where the stress in the market comes from this week: a bill for technical debt that was supposed to be deferred indefinitely has arrived all at once.

And the fifth thing is that the regulators are watching. Under NIS2, DORA and the SEC’s four-day disclosure rule, “we did not know we were running PHP” will be read as an admission.

The uncomfortable lessons

This embargo was handled by serious people with months of preparation, and it still leaked through a mistaken video upload and a vendor publishing early. Amazon saw exploitation attempts four days before anyone outside the circle was supposed to know. I would now treat any embargo as a courtesy. Plan on 24 to 48 hours of warning for the next one, and expect that warning to come from a honeypot rather than a mailing list.

The OOM flaw sat unfixed for six years because turning it into code execution looked impractical. Frontier models made it practical, so “not proven exploitable” should no longer be enough to close a ticket. The PHP Foundation has published 15 CVEs since July and says AI-assisted research is sending it far more reports than before. Every mature codebase written in C has a drawer full of bugs that were triaged as theoretical. That drawer is now being emptied, and not only by the people who will tell you about it.

Inventory was the control that mattered on Wednesday. Everyone was vulnerable, so the useful question was where PHP was running. The organisations that could answer that in minutes were patched within hours. The ones that could not are still discovering what they own, and they are discovering it in the same order the attackers are.

The sites that cannot be patched today were kept on old PHP because upgrading looked expensive and the risk looked abstract. For years that was a defensible trade-off. This week the risk became concrete, and the upgrade belongs on this quarter’s plan for anyone still running end-of-life runtimes on internet-facing systems.

The maintainers are carrying us. A handful of people at a foundation spent ten weeks fixing the engine that runs seventy percent of the web, under embargo, while watching that embargo fail around them. That arrangement held while bugs surfaced slowly. It will not hold once AI finds them faster than volunteers can fix them. Every enterprise that depends on PHP and does not fund the PHP Foundation is taking a free ride on infrastructure it would never accept for its own data centre.

What to do now

The next 72 hours are about containment. The next quarter is about never being in this position again.

In the next 72 hours

Find every PHP runtime you own, not every application you remember. Scan from the outside in. Include container images, serverless functions, appliances with embedded web interfaces, the marketing stack, acquired brands and anything an agency ever built for you. If you run Orca, the PHP2Shell news item in the platform includes a query that lists every asset with a PHP package installed across your connected cloud accounts.

Patch everything on 8.2 or later today, without waiting for a change window.

For 7.4 through 8.1, compile the backports or upgrade. For anything older, take it off the internet or put it behind a WAF with the PHP2Shell rules enabled, and accept that this is a bandage.

Assume compromise for any internet-facing PHP host that was unpatched after 17 October. In Orca, the PHP2Shell alerts flag which vulnerable hosts are reachable from the internet, so start there. Hunt for web shells, new admin users, modified core files and outbound connections you did not expect.

Rotate every secret that lived in PHP process memory on an exposed host: database credentials, API keys, cloud access keys, signing secrets.

Ask every vendor, agency and SaaS provider that touches your data the same question: which PHP version, patched when, and what did you find.

In the next quarter

Retire end-of-life PHP from anything internet-facing, with a budget line and an owner. If the application cannot move, treat the application itself as the risk.

Get secrets out of process memory. Short-lived credentials, workload identity and a secrets manager mean that the next memory-read bug leaks tokens that expire in an hour instead of keys that last for years.

Put an edge in front of everything. A CDN or WAF that can take a virtual patch in minutes bought the well-prepared organisations about eleven hours this week, which is often the difference between a hunt and a breach.

Create a pre-authorised emergency change path. The companies that patched within hours had already agreed, in calm times, who can push a change to production without a meeting.

Prioritise by exposure, not by CVSS. Two 9.2s on an internal admin tool behind a VPN are a Thursday. The same two on a public storefront holding card data are a board call. Your tooling should already know the difference.

How Orca can help

Most of the first 72 hours goes on finding out what you own, and that is where Orca starts. Orca’s agentless SideScanning reads installed packages directly from cloud workloads, so PHP is found on virtual machines, containers and container images without anything to deploy first. Detection for both CVEs went live in the platform on 21 October.

Finding PHP answers half of the question. The other half is deciding what to patch first and what an attacker could reach from each host. Each PHP2Shell alert shows whether the asset is reachable from the internet, whether the vulnerable component is loaded at runtime, and how critical it is to the business.

For the hunt and the clean-up, Orca’s lightweight eBPF Sensor adds runtime visibility on the hosts where it is deployed, and the asset graph shows which keys and cloud roles each exposed host holds, and that is where secret rotation should start.

Several customers told us the Early Intel query in the platform’s From the News item gave them a head start, letting them find their PHP hosts and begin mitigating before the official advisory went out.

None of this replaces patching. It shortens the time between the advisory and knowing where to patch first.

What this means for the next two years

PHP2Shell is the first widely visible instance of a pattern that will define vulnerability management for the rest of this decade.

AI has collapsed the cost of turning a theoretical bug into a working exploit. The backlog of “unproven” memory-safety issues in the foundational C codebases of the internet, the interpreters, the TLS libraries, the image parsers, the web servers, is enormous, and it was accumulated in an era when proving exploitability took a specialist a month. That era ended this summer. Expect the same story, with different names, in Python, Ruby, Node, OpenSSL and the kernel. Expect it more than once a quarter. Every CISO should assume their foundational dependencies have critical bugs. What they can still influence is whether they hear about them through a coordinated advisory or through an incident.

The window between disclosure and mass exploitation is now measured in hours, and sometimes it is negative. Monthly patch cycles were designed for a world where attackers needed weeks to weaponise a bug. For anything that faces the internet, that cadence is obsolete. The operating model that survives this decade treats patching exposed systems as a continuous process with a pre-approved fast lane, and treats a virtual patch at the edge as the normal first response rather than an exotic one. It also depends on an inventory that can answer “where do we run X” in a minute, across cloud, on-premises, containers, vendors and the long tail of forgotten sites.

If there is a single takeaway, it is about time. The weakness had been in PHP since 2012, the working exploit was about two months old, and the response had to happen within hours. The organisations under the most stress this week are the ones whose decision-making was built for a slower world, whatever the quality of their security teams. Most of what fixes that is deciding things in advance, so that the answers already exist before the next disclosure.
